text: Welcome aboard! On this opening slide you can see the problem statement sitting proudly in the middle—"integral of x times sine of two x, from zero to pi divided by eight".
Oh wow, a definite integral with both algebra and trig bundled together.
Exactly. Before we swing our chalk, let’s unpack what you’ll need in your toolbox—kind of like checking you have a map, a torch, and snacks before entering a cave.
Snacks? I’m in! What’s first on the checklist?
One—"integration by parts". Any time a lonely x is multiplied by a spicy trig function, that technique is our Swiss-army knife.
Got it. u v minus the integral of v d u, right?
Perfect recall. Two—basic trig integrals. We need to remember that the antiderivative of sine of two x is negative cosine of two x divided by two.
I can still hear my high-school teacher chanting that in my sleep.
Three—evaluating definite integrals. Once we have the antiderivative, we’ll plug in the upper limit pi divided by eight and the lower limit zero.
So the entire game plan is: choose u and d v cleverly, find v, rewrite, integrate again if needed, then slam in the limits.
That’s the roadmap. Quick warm-up question: looking at the first bullet under the problem, which factor would you nominate as u so that its derivative simplifies nicely?
I’d let u equal x because its derivative is just one—super simple.
Exactly—like choosing the lightest backpack for the hike. Great job! Anything feel mysterious so far?
Nope, just eager to try the parts formula.
Wonderful. Let’s stride to the next slide and set up the integration by parts.
On this slide the left column shows our choices: u equals x, d v equals sine of two x d x.
Which means d u is simply d x, and v is… let me integrate sine of two x…
Go for it—remember the chain rule when integrating.
The antiderivative should be negative cosine of two x divided by two.
Spot on. Many students forget that divide-by-two factor—cheeky little gremlin!
So plugging into u v minus integral v d u, I get x times negative cosine two x divided by two, minus the integral of negative cosine two x divided by two times d x.
Nicely stated. Notice how two negatives will eventually turn that second term positive.
Aha—minus a minus is plus. Algebraic sunshine!
Indeed. Pause and glance at the green highlight on the slide—see that fraction one over two? That’s the crucial constant travelling with us.
Right. Forgetting it would be like leaving the torch batteries at home.
Exactly, and we’d stumble in the dark. Anything you’d adjust before we continue?
I think we’re set. The first term is clear, the remaining integral is one half times the integral of cosine of two x.
Excellent. Let’s move on to simplifying that remaining integral.
Here the algebra unfolds. Focus on the line where the minus sign vanished.
Yup, we now have negative x times cosine of two x divided by two, evaluated from zero to pi over eight, plus one half integral of cosine two x d x.
Good. Want to handle that cosine integral?
Sure. The antiderivative of cosine two x is sine two x divided by two.
Perfect. Don’t lose the one half in front.
So the whole piece becomes one half times sine two x divided by two—that is sine two x over four.
Exactly—like stacking two filters: first one half, then another one half.
So we’ve traded a tougher integral for simpler functions we can plug limits into.
That’s the magic of integration by parts—turns a boulder into two small pebbles.
Pebbles ready! I’m itching to evaluate at the bounds.
Fantastic enthusiasm. Slide four, here we come.
The blackboard now shows F of x equals negative x cosine two x divided by two plus sine two x over four.
Upper limit first: x equals pi over eight. I’ll compute cosine of two x—that’s cosine of pi over four.
Which equals root two divided by two. Nicely spotted on the right-hand margin.
And sine of pi over four is also root two over two.
Symmetry can be beautiful, can’t it?
Plugging in, I get negative pi over eight times root two over two, all over two… Wait, let me write it neatly: negative pi times root two over thirty-two.
Good catch combining the denominators. And the second term becomes root two over two divided by four, which is root two over eight.
So F of pi over eight equals root two times four minus pi, all over thirty-two.
Very tidy! Now evaluate at the lower limit zero.
Easy—both pieces vanish, so F of zero is zero.
Therefore the definite integral is F of pi over eight minus zero, giving exactly what you just wrote.
That would be positive, right? Because four is bigger than pi.
Yes, about zero point eight six units bigger. Great internal check.
Awesome—answer in hand! What’s next—sanity check?
You read my mind. Final slide incoming.
Last slide: we list two quick validations. First, sign analysis—x is non-negative, sine of two x is non-negative on the interval, so area should be positive.
And our result root two times four minus pi over thirty-two is positive. Check!
Second, curriculum reflection. We successfully used "integration by parts" from the Integration—Continued unit.
Plus some chain-rule trig differentiation from the Functions and Differentiation unit.
Exactly. Quick numerical approximation—pop that into your calculator.
Crunching… I get about zero point zero three eight.
Reasonable magnitude for a small slice under the curve—great sanity tick.
Feels satisfying, like closing a well-written detective novel.
Beautiful analogy, Sherlock. Any lingering mysteries?
None—just proud of taming the integral dragon.
And you did it with flair! Keep that confidence for future adventures.
Thanks, mentor. Ready to tackle the next quest!
Fantastic. Until then, great job and take care.
